newsitem.title: MEXICO: Banco de Mexico net reserves, assets rise.
newsitem.headline: Banco de Mexico net reserves, assets rise.

text.p: Banco de Mexico said on Tuesday its net international reserves as of Feb. 28 rose to $20.202 billion, compared to $19.592 billion the week before.
The central bank said that its net international assets on the same date reached $10.472 billion, compared to $9.329 billion as of Feb 21.
The central bank said the increase of $1.143 billion in net international assets in the same time period was due to:

--Foreign exchange purchases from the government for $892 million, coming from the acquisition of foreign debt. Of this, $590 million was used to to pay off Banco de Mexico liabilities to the International Monetary Fund. It noted that payment did not affect the level of international assets because gross assets and liabilities changed by the same degree.
--The purchase of $148 million from financial institutions, a product of the partial exercising of options on the sale of dollars to the central bank that were issued on Feb. 21.
-- Net income from operations with state oil company Pemex worth $89 million.

--A let gain of $14 million dollars for a combination of factors including changes in the dollar value of non-dollar assets and liabilities held by the bank; net returns on interest rates and from trading of metals and securities; and net deposits in dollar accounts from commercial banks at the central bank.
Banco de Mexico said that between Feb. 21 and Feb. 28, the monetary base rose by 2.417 billion pesos due to a rise in the seasonal demand of bills and coins to pay month-end salaries.
The following table details Banco de Mexico's reserves and net domestic credit. All figures are in billions of pesos, unless otherwise indicated.
Feb. 21 Feb. 28
International Reserves
U.S. Dollars $19.592 bln $20.202 bln
Monetary Base 73.550 75.967
Net International Assets*
U.S. Dollars $9.329 bln $10.472 bln
Net Domestic Credit 1.144 -7.537
*Net International Assets are defined as gross international assets minus central bank liabilities with the IMF and assets of less than a six-month duration from other central banks.
